title: Cu-CuOx/rGO catalyst derived from hybrid LDH/GO with enhanced C2H4 selectivity by CO2 electrochemical reduction
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 conversion to value-added fuels and chemicals enabled by suitable heterogeneous catalysts has attained great attention given its economic viability and overall process efficiency. Herein, we have designed a new electro-catalyst ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO using electro-reduction method from Cu5Al-CO3 hybrid LDH/GO precursor for efficient CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). Interestingly, the ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalyst presented a higher C2H4 production selectivity than the ER-Cu5-LDH catalyst without rGO. The obtained ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO exhibited a high C2H4 faradaic efficiency (FE) up to 54 % and a high C2H4 partial current density of ‒11.64 mA/ cm at ‒1.2 V vs. RHE. It also exhibited excellent stability up to 50 h. The total FE of gaseous and liquid products for ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO is closed to 100 %. The morphological changes during CO2RR were monitored using SEM analyses for catalyst stability examination. The influence of electrolyte or pH on the electro-catalytic performance of ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO were studied. In order to reflect the superiority of LDH precursors, a control catalyst containing Cu2O supported on rGO (ER-Cu2O/rGO) was prepared and comparatively studied. Overall, our hybrid catalyst system ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO is very promising materials for CO2 conversion to C2H4, displaying remarkable FE, high C2H4 partial current density, and the excellent stability. Such a commendable behavior is ascribed to the excellent dispersion of active copper species as well as the superior electric conductivity of rGO.

A B S T R A C T

Such a commendable behavior is ascribed to the excellent dispersion of active copper species as well as the superior electric conductivity of rGO.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Renewable energy sources such as solar, wind and hydroelectricity have attracted increasing attention with the great potential to at least partially replace fossil fuels, but long-term energy storage still remains a big challenge to meet the worldwide energy demand [1,2]. Presently, carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction reaction (CO2RR) which converts CO2 to value-added fuels provides an energy storage solution to combat the energy crisis [3,4]. As a consequence, a plethora of studies dealing with nanostructured metal-based catalytic materials have been conducted showcasing the potential of electro-chemical routes for CO2 reduction [5–14]. Unfortunately, there is not a fully optimized catalytic formulation to achieve success results and in many occasions, the selected catalysts fail to display enough activity, selectivity and/or stability towards the desired upgrading products. In this quest, further investigation is needed to design a new generation of advanced CO2RR catalysts
with high selectivity and activity toward added value products [15–17]. To date, Cu-based electro-catalysts are the most investigated cata-
lyst systems for CO2RR since they are economically appealing and typically display a great potential for selective C2 production [18,19]. For instance, the oxide-derived Cu-based catalysts are considered to be efficient for multi-carbon (C–C) selective production during CO2RR [20–24]. Detailed studies revealed that the residual oxides within the catalysts play a vital role in catalytic performance, and these oxides still exist even after CO2RR.7 However, the pristine oxidized Cu nanoparticles are prone to sinter thus reducing the surface to volume ratio and hindering the exposure of surface active sites. In addition, Cu (I) or Cu (II) present at oxidized Cu nanocrystals may undergo reduction resulting in less active Cu (0) species during long-term CO2RR process [20,25]. Thus, the poor stability of the oxidized Cu electro-catalysts in aqueous solution at reducing electrochemical potentials poses a major unresolved challenge within the CO2RR processes.

Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) is a group of 2D layered materials containing exchangeable anions with an adjustable cation composition,12,13 which have already been investigated in many advanced applications such as CO2 capture [26], nitrogen oxides (NOx) removal [27], volatile organic compound (VOC) removal [28], thermal catalysis for CO2 conversion [29], electro-catalysis [30], and photo-catalysis, etc [31–33]. Recently, our team reported a copper-based catalyst (CuCu2O) electro-derived from Cu-based LDH for C2 selective production [34]. This catalyst contained a small amount of Cu2O even after CO2RR and exhibited a C2H4 FE of 36 % and an excellent stability levels up to 20 h. We considered such distinctive approach for electro-derived composite from LDHs with well-mixed fine nanoparticles would represent an adequate starting point to develop oxygen combined copper catalysts for C-C coupling during CO2RR. Nevertheless, the LDH derived composites exhibited low current density. To overcome this problem, we propose that assembling the LDH derived Cu-Cu2O catalyst with carbon material can improve its electric conductivity, leading to higher current density and electro-catalytic activity [35,36].
Graphene oxide (GO) has oxygenic functional groups that can enhance the oxidation reaction. By a further reduction modification, lots of continuous change in geometry (topological defects) and carbon vacancies can be generated over the reduced graphene oxide (rGO), which may enhance the sorption, intercalation and activation of ions and molecules [37]. Indeed due to its excellent electric conductivity, high mechanical strength and stability, rGO has been well studied as catalyst support for electro-catalysis [35]. Indeed, successful examples can be found in literature dealing with LDHs/rGO composites applied to
NOx reduction, oxygen evolution reaction and oxygen reduction reaction [38]. Moreover, many rGO based copper and its oxides nano-particles have been investigated for CO2RR [25,39,40]. Under these premises, we were inspired to design a novel Cu-based catalyst from LDH/ rGO hybrid composite with high electric conductivity for efficient C2 products formation by CO2RR.
In this scenario, our work showcases the successful development of a novel electro-catalyst ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO prepared by electrochemical reduction of LDH/GO composites for CO2 electrochemical reduction. This advanced catalyst has been compared to reference materials. Our multicomponent catalyst exhibited excellent C2H4 selectivity by suppressing hydrogen evolution reaction along with high current density. Among all the tested electro-catalysts, the ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO showed the highest C2H4 FE of 54 % and excellent stability of 50 h for C2H4 production at an applied potential of ‒1.2 V vs. RHE. Hence, we believe this novel ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO electro-catalyst derived from the LDH/GO hybrid represents an advanced alternative for C2H4 production from CO2.

sections.heading: 2.1.1. Preparation of Cu5Al-CO3 LDH/GO and Cu2O/GO composites
sections.text:
The hybrid Cu5Al-CO3 LDH/GO was prepared through a co-precipitation technique at room temperature. 0.2 g GO into (100 ml) of water, was stirred and sonicated for 2 h respectively and then 0.05 mol
Na2CO3 was slowly added into the same solution for 10 min. Subsequently, a solution was prepared by mixing 0.125 mol Cu (NO3)2·6H2O and 0.025 mol Al(NO3)3·9H2O in 100 mL water. Then, this solution was added dropwise into 100 mL alkaline solution containing 0.2 g GO and 0.05 mol Na2CO3 under stirring. During the whole preparation process, NaOH solution (4 M) was added dropwise to keep the pH at 10. The obtained solution followed stirrer up to 12 h for aging of precipitate. After 12 h, the mixture was first filtered and then ensured the pH became 7 by washing with DI-water. Later on, the obtained precipitate was washed with C2H5OH and followed 2 h stirring process, which is meant to improve the composite particles dispersion. The number “5” in ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalyst is the Cu/Al molar ratio.
The Cu2O/GO catalyst was prepared at room temperature by slowly adding 0.2 g GO into 100 ml DI-water and sonicated for 3 h. Then, the obtained solution was stirred for 2 h and 0.312 mol (4.50 g) commercial Cu2O was slowly added during stirring. The resulting solution was further sonicated for 6 h. The final solution with precipitates was filtered and first washed with DI-water for several times and then, with C2H5OH for best dispersion. The precipitant was dried in oven at 40 ºC for 3 h.

sections.heading: 2.1.2. Preparation of catalysts by electro-reduction method
sections.text:
Firstly, the commercial carbon cloth (CC) with a size of 1.5 × 1.5 cm2 was treated in the solution containing 5% H2SO4 and 95 % H2O for 20 min and washed with DI-water to attain neutral pH. Then, the obtained carbon cloth was dried at room temperature and weighted before loading. Then, 60 mg as-prepared LDH, LHD/GO, or Cu2O/GO sample, 30 μL 5% Nafion solution and 1 mL C2H5OH were together mixed and sonicated for 2 h for better dispersion. Afterward, the dropwise method is used to load and spread out the mixture on carbon paper, then dried under heating lamp. Catalysts loaded on CC were subsequently electrochemical reduced by applying a potential (‒1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl) for 2 h to obtain the derived electro-reduced catalysts. The LDH derived catalyst was noted ER-Cu5-LDH, the LDH/GO derived catalyst was noted as ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO, and the Cu2O/GO derived catalyst was
named as ER-Cu2O/rGO. Electro-polishing of Cu foil was done as described in our previous work [34].

sections.heading: 2.2. Material characterizations
sections.text: Scanning-electron-microscopy (SEM) was conducted in a HITACHI SU8010 apparatus using the acceleration voltage of SEM is 300 kV and high-resolution-transmission-electron-microscopy (HR-TEM) was conducted in a FEI Tecnai-G2 TF20 microscope with 200 kV FEG high resolution. Both techniques were used to observe the morphological changes, d-spacing and SAED analysis of samples. X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Shimadzu XRD-7000) with Cu-Kα radiation was used to analyze the crystal structure and crystallinity of samples. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo-Fischer ESCALAB 250Xi) using monochromatic Al-Kα (1486.6 eV) radiation was used for surface analysis of samples, which was calibrated with C 1s peak (284.6 eV). For XPS analysis, the samples without exposing to air are immediately rinsed with DI water (pH = 7), dried in N2 flow gas and vacuum packed to avoid any impurity.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
First, 40 mg as-prepared catalyst was inter-mixed with 10 μL 5% Nafion solution and 1 mL C2H5OH at room temperature, and then sonicated for 1 h to obtain a well-dispersed ink. The working electrode was prepared by spreading 35 μL as-prepared ink onto the glassy carbon electrode with 6 mm diameter, which was then dried under a heating lamp. Moreover, the calibrated Ag/AgCl as reference electrode and Pt meshes as counter electrode were applied for a three-electrode system, respectively. Current density is the amount of electric current flowing per unit cross-sectional area of a material. ECSA is the area of the electrode material that is accessible to the electrolyte that is used for charge transfer and/or storage. Electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of catalysts was measured in 0.5 KHCO3 through a series of cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements in a potential range of (−0.35
∼ −0.55 V vs. Ag/AgCl) under five scan rates (20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 mV s−1). The double layer capacitance was determined by getting the slop from the graph plotted between geometric current density as a function of scan rate. Reaction products and remaining reactants were on-line monitored using gas chromatography (GC2014C) facilitated equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) for H2 and CO detection and two flame ionization detectors (FID) for CH4 and C2H4 detection. The analysis was of the gas products was conducted every 7.5 min. Subsequently, the calculation method for CO2RR products analysis is same to our previous work, except for the applied potential range of ‒0.9 V ∼ ‒1.7 V (vs. RHE). [34] In CO2 electrochemical reduction reaction the highly selective product means that a catalyst can direct a particular reaction to yield a specific product. However, in CO2RR the FE is taken in account to validate the selective product during reaction by following equation.
= × αnF Q FE(%) 100 total
where α is the number of electrons transferred, which is 2 for CO and H2, n is the number of moles for a given product (detected by GC), mol;
F is the Faraday's constant (96485 C mol−1), Q is the total of all the charge passed throughout the electrolysis process (measured by the potentiostat).
2.4. Liquid products identification
The obtained liquid products in electrolyte were analyzed by 1H NMR spectroscopy (700 MHz spectrometer BRUKER AVANCE III HD). The internal standard (IS) was dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, SigmaAldrich, 99.9 %) and phenol (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.0 %∼100.5 %) in D2O (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9 atom %D). The water peak was suppressed by presaturation sequence. Further, the ratio of peak areas for other products were compared with that of DMSO.

sections.heading: 3.1. Preparation and characterization of electro-catalysts
sections.text:
In this contribution, two Cu-based electro-catalysts ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO were prepared by ECR of Cu5Al-CO3 LDHs and Cu5Al-
CO3 LDH/GO. The structural properties of materials were first investigated by XRD analyses. Fig. 1a shows that the XRD patterns of asprepared Cu5Al-CO3 LDH and Cu5Al-CO3 LDH/GO hybrids. The characteristic XRD peaks evidence the presence of multiple family of planes at 11.7° (003), 23.8° (006), 34.7° (009), 39.8° (015), and 47.9° (015) which are assigned to LDHs reflections (JCPDS #46-0099) [41]. Upon electrochemical reduction of the catalyst, copper species including Cu, Cu2O and CuO appeared in ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalysts. The characteristic peaks of Cu were observed in both catalysts at 43.1°, 50.2° and 74.1°, corresponding to the reflections of (111), (200) and (220) copper planes patterns (JCPDS #04-0836). The three observed peaks were consistent with copper foil peak pattern. The same
derived catalyst also has the characteristic peaks of Cu2O at 36.3° and 61.6°, referring to the reflections of (111) and (220) planes (JCPDS #78-2076). Besides, CuO peaks at 32.4°, 35.6° and 38.7° were observed in ER-Cu5-LDH, referring to the reflections of (110), (111) and (002) planes, respectively (JCPDS #45-0937).
An overall picture of the surface chemistry and the surface chemical composition of the prepared samples was obtained by XPS. For the ERCu5-LDH/rGO sample, the sp2C (C = C), sp3c (C–C) and C–O–C peaks were clearly observed in the C1s spectra (Fig. 1b), confirming the existence of rGO. Fig. 1c shows the Cu 2p spectra of electro-catalysts, from which no much difference (only 0.1 eV difference) could be observed in Cu+ and Cu° during Cu 2px binding energy. [42,43] Hence, Cu LMM
Auger spectra was further analyzed to distinguish between Cu+ and Cu° species (Fig. 1d). The Auger spectra reflected that Cu2O (or Cu+) auger peak at 569.9–570.0 eV in all electro-catalysts. These characterization analyses revealed that the Cu2+ in LDH could be reduced into Cu and Cu2O under the electro-reduction condition. These are interesting results since Cu+ (3d10) and Cu (3d104s1) are electronically suitable species to activate CO2 by electron donation to its antibonding orbitals thus facilitating the catalytic process.
The morphological transmutations of Cu-based LDH and Cu-based LDH/GO samples before and after ECR-treatment were studied by means of SEM. Cu5Al-CO3 LDH and Cu5Al-CO3 LDH/GO exhibited
flower-like morphology with ultrathin-nano-sheets acting as petals (Fig. 2a-b). After the electro-reduction treatment, ER-Cu5-LDH and ERCu5-LDH/rGO exhibited different morphologies. ER-Cu5-LDH showed nano-dendrites morphology (Fig. 2c), while ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO was composed of spherical nanoparticles with an average measured size of 200−500 nm (Fig. 2d). The morphologies of ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO and ERCu5-LDH were further studied by HR-TEM analyses (Fig. 3), in which the presence of rGO in ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO was observed. Moreover, the co-existence of Cu, Cu2O (and CuO) in the electro-derived catalysts were confirmed from the d-spacing and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) in the HR-TEM analyses (Fig. 3c-d). The d-spacing of 0.181
nm and 0.209 nm could be assigned to the (200) and (111) planes of Cu, [44,45] the d-spacing of 0.148 nm and 0.246 nm was attributed to the (220) and (111) planes of Cu2O, [44,45] while the d-spacing of 0.275 nm is ascribed to the (110) plane of CuO [46]. Subsequently, the SAED patterns of both catalysts were recorded in corresponding to d-spacing, for existing of Cu, Cu2O (and CuO). The SAED analysis further confirmed the presence of different Cu and its oxides in the as prepared
catalysts. Hence, the SAED analysis of both catalysts is consistent with the conclusions extracted from the XRD patterns (Fig. 1a).

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical performance evaluation for CO2RR
sections.text:
The electrochemical performance toward CO2RR of ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO were comparatively investigated through linear
sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves in both N2 and CO2 concentrated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolytes at a sweeping rate of 50 mV/s (Fig. 4a). It can be observed that both catalysts exhibited higher current densities in CO2 saturated electrolyte than those in N2 saturated electrolyte, suggesting the CO2 reduction reaction took place. Besides, the ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO
exhibited higher negative current density than ER-Cu5-LDH at applied potential (‒1.2 V vs. RHE) in CO2 saturated electrolyte (0.1 M KHCO3), suggesting this catalyst is more efficient for CO2RR. Furthermore, the CO2RR gaseous product distributions of ER-Cu5-LDH, ER-Cu5-LDH/ rGO, and comparatively, Cu-foil were studied at a potential range of ‒0.9 ∼ ‒1.7 V vs. RHE in an H-type cell (Fig. 4b-c, Fig. S1). The Cu-foil as reference material, always prefers CH4 formation in the potential range (−0.9 ∼ −1.7 V vs. RHE), and both the CO and C2H4 selectivity were lower than 12 % (Fig. S1a). However, compared to Cu-foil, the production of CH4 in ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalysts was remarkably suppressed (especially at lower potentials) and the C2H4 production was obviously improved in the entire potential range. Besides, both ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalysts achieved their maximum value of C2H4 FE at −1.2 V vs. RHE, which was 54 % and 44.8 % for ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO and ER-Cu5-LDH, respectively. Interestingly, no CH4 formation was detected at this potential showcasing the enhanced selective of our multicomponent catalysts for C2 products. The liquid products are identified via NMR analysis and calculated (Fig. 5a-b). The total FE (%) of gaseous products (C2H4 = 54.7, CO = 11.1, H2 = 21.2) and liquid products (HCOOH= 9, C2H5OH= 3.2 and negligible amount of other products) for ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO was closed to 100 %. Moreover, the partial and total current densities of electrocatalysts were analyzed (Fig. 4d-e). ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO showed higher total current density compared to ER-Cu5-LDH in the entire potential range, an observation that is consistent with the LSV results. Thus, ER-
Cu5-LDH/rGO achieved a maximum C2H4 partial current density of 11.64 mA/cm2 at −1.2 V vs. RHE, showing higher activity towards C2H4 production than that exhibited by ER-Cu5-LDH (6.82 mA/cm2).
The electrochemical behavior of the engineered materials was further characterized by comparing their electrochemical active surface areas (ECSAs) estimated through CV. The capacitance of ER-Cu5-LDH/ rGO (520 μF/cm2) was comparatively analyzed to be higher than ERCu5-LDH (401 μF/cm2) (Fig. 4f, Fig. S2a-b), indicating ER-Cu5-LDH/ rGO possesses higher ECSA greater concentration of active sites exposed in the surface for CO2RR. The later consequently result in high activity and commendable C2H4 production performance. To investigate the catalytic efficiency regarding to charge transfer kinetics, the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of electro-catalysts was measured to determine the semi-circle radii, which represent the transport of charge and its conductivity at the interface of electrode and electrolyte. ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO had smaller semicircle radius than ER-Cu5LDH (Fig. 5c), indicating that it has higher charge transfer efficiency that can lead to excellent CO2RR performance. The Tafel slopes were also used to measure the reaction kinetics (Fig. 5d). ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO showed a Tafel slope of 65.4 mV dec−1, which is less than that for ERCu5-LDH (88.8 mV dec−1). It indicates that ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO possesses a faster electron transfer rate leading to a faster reaction kinetics in CO2RR. This effect is consistent with the integral activity depicted by the LSV curves (Fig. 4a). Higher Tafel slope implies that a higher over potential is required to start the catalytic reaction.
Considering the stability is also an important parameter for electrochemical CO2 reduction, the long-term electro-catalytic evaluation of ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalysts were studied at −1.2 V vs. RHE (Fig. 6). It can be seen that ER-Cu5-LDH maintained a stable behavior up to 22 h and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO presented an excellent stability of 50 h in both total current density and C2H4 FE. To further investigate the stability of these two catalysts, SEM images of these catalysts after CO2RR at different reaction times are shown in Fig. 7. As evidenced in the images, after 11 h operation, only slight changes were observed within ER-Cu5-LDH and ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO samples treated under the same conditions. Interestingly, the ER-Cu5-LDH morphology started to deteriorate after 22 h operation. While the morphology of ERCu5-LDH/rGO remained almost unchanged during CO2RR and only slightly modifications take place after 30 h of continuous operation.
Aiming to establish a meaningful comparison and benchmark our catalysts compared to reference materials, the performance of ER-Cu5LDH/rGO was compared with literature reported Cu-based catalysts. The C2H4 FE, C2H4 partial current density, and stability were selected as contrast metrics and they are summarized in Table 1 and Table S1. Such a comparison clearly showcases that our ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalyst exhibited a quite high C2H4 FE and partial current density and displayed a remarkable durability when contrasted to state of the art catalysts.
Electrochemical properties of the reaction media may also affect the catalytic behavior. In this vein, the effects of the electrolyte and pH were studied for the ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalyst. Herein, CO2RR was carried out in CO2 concentrated 0.1 M KCl electrolyte (pH of 3.9). The C2H4 production selectivity was found to be very low (lower than 20 %) and showed a decreasing trend during 11 h of operation (Fig. 8). From these results, it was conceived that the nature of electrolyte and pH value strongly influenced the catalytic performance towards C2H4 production. Indeed, pH can affect the adsorption and interaction of key intermediate species (CO* or H*) on the catalysts surface. Additionally, the effect of pH is ascribed to the thermodynamic balanced of the copper surface through the negative repulsive electrostatic force [47]. Furthermore, ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO was also conducted in Ar gas flow in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (Fig. S3). Under this situation, only HER was observed without any CO2 reduction products (CO, CH4 or C2H4 etc). These results reflected that carbonaceous products obtained in CO2RR are indeed derived from CO2 gas instead of other carbon compounds in electrolyte or catalyst.
Aiming to further highlight the superiority of LDH precursors, a control catalyst containing Cu2O supported on rGO (ER-Cu2O/rGO) was prepared and comparatively studied. The prepared ER-Cu2O/rGO was first studied by XRD analyses, which showed similar pattern with ERCu5-LDH/rGO (Fig. 9a). The CO2RR performance of ER-Cu2O/rGO catalyst was evaluated under the same conditions to ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO CO2RR (Fig. 9b-d). As per observed for ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO, the ER-Cu2O/ rGO sample also achieved its highest C2H4 FE at −1.2 V vs. RHE. During 90 min CO2RR operation, the C2H4, H2 and CO FE over ERCu2O/rGO was 27 %, 37 %, and 20 %, respectively. Particularly, the C2H4 FE over ER-Cu2O/rGO (27 %) is much lower than that over ERCu5-LDH/rGO (54 %). ER-Cu2O/rGO also showed less current density that exhibited by ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO (Fig. 9d). Further, the ECSA of two catalysts were comparatively analyzed which is illustrated the ERCu2O/rGO has 165 μF/cm2 which is very less that ECSA value of ERCu5-LDH/rGO (520 μF/cm2). Cu-based LDH/GO derived nanoparticles highly dispersed in the rGO layered, while the nanoparticles derived from hybrid Cu2O/rGO are not well dispersed on the layered structure. This may be due to the active copper species in ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO being better dispersed given the unique structure of LDH precursor [34].

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
We have designed a new electro-catalyst ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO by ECR of Cu5Al-CO3 LDH/GO with promising features for electrochemical CO2 upgrading. XRD and XPS analyses indicated that ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO contains both Cu and Cu2O active species. Both active species are electronically suitable to conduct the reaction rate limiting step: CO2 activation. SEM analyses revealed that ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO maintained its morphology during CO2RR and only slightly deformed after 30 h operation. ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO achieved a C2H4 FE up to 54 % at −1.2 V vs. RHE, which was much higher than the control catalysts ER-Cu5-LDH (44.8 %) and Cu-foil (< 12 %). Very importantly, no CH4 formation was detected over ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO at −1.2 V vs. RHE indicating the enhanced selectivity of our catalysts for C2 products. Indeed, the ERCu5-LDH/rGO displayed a maximum C2H4 partial current density of 11.64 mA/cm2 at −1.2 V vs. RHE, higher than that of ER-Cu5-LDH (6.82 mA/cm2). The Tafel slope of ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO suggested that it possesses a faster electron transfer rate, which can lead to a faster reaction kinetics in CO2RR. ER-Cu5-LDH/rGO catalyst also showed an excellent stability of 50 h in both total current density and C2H4 FE. Our study also reveals that the nature of electrolyte and pH value can strongly influence the catalytic performance toward C2H4 production. The rGO improve the electric conductivity and performance of catalyst. The superiority of LDH precursor was confirmed by comparing ER-Cu5LDH/rGO with a control catalyst containing Cu2O supported on rGO (ER-Cu2O/rGO). We believe that the active copper species in ER-Cu5LDH/rGO display enhanced dispersion due to the unique structure of LDH precursor, resulting in a remarkable positive impact in the catalytic behavior. Overall, our work showcases the promising behavior of Cu-supported on hybrid LDH/rGO materials for electrochemical conversion of CO2. The chemistry and unique structural properties of this custom-made catalysts make then suitable to yield added C2 products paving the way to develop innovative solutions to facilitate the transition towards a low-carbon future.
